Revised assessment with literature context:
The FOMC statement acknowledges a negative supply shock—energy/food and war-related disruptions—pushing inflation up while weighing on activity. Empirically, VAR evidence (Sims 1992) and standard DSGE/Phillips-curve frameworks imply that tightening the policy rate to 2.25–2.5% and proceeding with balance-sheet reduction will restrain demand and lower inflation, but with short-run output costs. Sticky-information dynamics (Mankiw and Reis 2002) suggest inflation persistence, so the Committee’s emphasis on “ongoing increases” and credibility can help realign expectations, limiting the sacrifice ratio relative to an uncredible stance. The statement’s strong anti-inflation commitment is consistent with the welfare-cost arguments of Feldstein (1978, 1998), and its data-dependent language reflects lessons from Orphanides on mismeasured slack in the 1970s. Historically, credible disinflation (the Volcker episode) shows that resolute action can lower long-term inflation expectations, partially offsetting near-term negativity. Balancing these, the war-driven supply shock and immediate growth headwinds are negative, while robust recent job gains and credible anti-inflation policy are positives. Net tone: moderately negative, less severe than a purely “stagflationary” read.
